blocks.text: Two classic questions that turn out to be the **same algorithm**, so they share one lesson:

items: **Same Tree** — given the roots `p` and `q` of two binary trees, return `true` if they are **identical**: the same shape and the same value at every position.
**Symmetric Tree** — given the `root` of one binary tree, return `true` if it is a **mirror of itself** around its centre.

blocks.alt: Left: two identical trees, 1 with children 2 and 3; matching positions are compared. Right: a symmetric tree 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3; the left half mirrors the right half, so mirrored positions are compared: 3 with 3 on the outside, 4 with 4 on the inside.

blocks.code:
Same Tree:      p = [1, 2, 3],  q = [1, 2, 3]   -> true
                p = [1, 2],     q = [1, null, 2] -> false   (same values, different shape)
Symmetric Tree: root = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3]     -> true
                root = [1, 2, 2, null, 3, null, 3] -> false

blocks.text: Here's the connection. To check two trees are the same, compare them **position by position**: the roots, then left with left and right with right. A tree is symmetric when its **left subtree is the mirror of its right subtree** — the same comparison, except the pairs are **crossed**: left with right, and right with left.

blocks.alt: Which pairs are compared next. Same Tree compares a.left with b.left and a.right with b.right. Symmetric Tree compares a.left with b.right (the outside pair) and a.right with b.left (the inside pair).

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: turn the trees into text

**Same Tree:** write each tree out as a string that captures both values and shape — preorder, with a `#` for every missing child — and compare the strings. **Symmetric Tree:** build a **mirrored copy** of the tree and check it's the same as the original.

**Time O(n · h), space O(n).** Every level of recursion copies its children's strings, and the whole of both trees is processed even when the very first values differ. Without the `#` markers it would be wrong: `[1, 2]` and `[1, null, 2]` have the same preorder values.
2. Optimal: compare pairs with a queue

Compare as you go instead of building anything. Put the first pair in a queue. Take pairs out: two nulls match; one null, or different values, means **false** immediately. Otherwise add their children's pairs — **straight** pairs for Same Tree, **crossed** pairs for Symmetric Tree.
**Time O(n), space O(w)** — and it **stops at the first mismatch** instead of processing whole trees.
3. Best solution: the same comparison, recursively

Written recursively, each function is three lines: both empty → match; one empty or different values → no match; otherwise both child pairs must match. Symmetric Tree just calls the mirror version on the root's two children.

blocks.alt: The recursive mirror check on 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3. isMirror(2, 2) checks the values, then isMirror(3, 3) for the outside pair and isMirror(4, 4) for the inside pair.

blocks.caption: Try the two failing examples: one breaks on shape, one on a value.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)**, stopping at the first mismatch — `&&` doesn't even look at the inside pair if the outside pair already failed. This is the answer interviewers expect; the queue version is the follow-up for "without recursion".

rows.approach: Brute force: turn the trees into text
rows.timeWhy: Every level of recursion **copies its children's strings**, and both whole trees are processed.

rows.approach: Optimal: compare pairs with a queue
rows.timeWhy: Each pair of nodes is compared **once**, stopping at the **first mismatch**.
rows.spaceWhy: The queue holds about **one level** of pairs.

items: **Same values, different shape** — `[1, 2]` vs `[1, null, 2]`: `false`. The null checks catch it.
**Symmetric shape, wrong values** — `[1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3]`: `false` on the inside pair.
**Subtree of Another Tree** — is any subtree of one tree the *same tree* as the other? (Its own lesson, using this check.)
**Flip Equivalent Binary Trees** — the same, but at each node either the straight or the crossed pairing may match.
**Leaf-Similar Trees** — compare only the sequence of leaves.
**Invert Binary Tree** — a tree is symmetric exactly when inverting it changes nothing.
